glossary.plain: The fastest this GPU allows for this model: the time to move every byte the step needs once at the GPU's memory speed (or, for heavy maths, at its top compute speed). A real run is always slower.
Milliseconds: thousandths of a second.
The text the model reads before it starts to reply. Reading it is called prefill.
One piece of the model's work in each step, such as the feed-forward or attention layers, or the time between GPU steps.
How long this part takes now, in each token (or each step of several streams, or each prompt).
This part's share of the lost time: of all the time the run takes beyond the limit, how much is in this part.
What this part would give back if it ran at its own limit: its share of the distance from the measured speed to the limit.
A part's time now, less its time at the limit.
The fastest this kind of work can run on this GPU by any method, not only the engine's.
Gigabytes a second: how fast memory is read.
How much of the GPU's top maths speed a part uses.
Time between GPU kernels, when the GPU waits for the next piece of work.
A tool that watches the GPU and notes when every kernel starts and ends. Watching slows the run a little.
The run with no recording tool attached: the speed the engine really has.
How the model's numbers are stored: fewer bits per number means less to read and a faster step, at some cost in accuracy.
What the model keeps about earlier tokens (keys and values), read again for every new token.
The part of the model that looks back at earlier tokens.
The largest part of each layer: two big matrix steps on every token.
Layers that carry a running summary of the conversation instead of looking back at every token.
The program that runs the model (llama.cpp, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM or tinygrad).
The engine's version. The pin is the version BoltBeam was last checked against; upstream is the newest release.
The GPU driver and libraries the engine was built with.

lines: The speed is the engine running on its own, with nothing recording it, on the run's own prompt.
Recording slowed the run by 1.5% (the limit is 5%).
The limit is the sum of each recorded part's own fastest time on this GPU.
A part with no limit of its own counts all of its time as lost.

time_budget.line: Where the 1,700.0 ms of the traced request (under the profiler) went: GPU kernels 1,344.4 ms, copies with no kernel running 261.3 ms, GPU idle 163.5 ms; the host time before and after the GPU work is unknown. These do not add up: the trace's GPU work (1,769.2 ms) is longer than the request's wall time, so the trace holds more than this one request.
lines: The parts exceed the wall by 69.2 ms.

Of the GPU idle time, CPU work (no GPU API call in flight) took 158.4 ms; a copy call the host waits in took 0.2 ms; the host waiting for the GPU (synchronize) took 0.1 ms; 4.8 ms is in 8,820 short gaps under 1 ms each.

Kernel time by family: dense matrix multiplies 329.2 ms, expert matrix multiplies 304.4 ms, elementwise kernels (norms, type conversion) 227.0 ms, attention 118.6 ms, recurrent layers 118.6 ms, other kernels 103.7 ms, expert routing and combine 88.5 ms, copies and gathers 54.4 ms.
Host-to-GPU copies from pinned host memory on GPU queue 15: 17.42 GB in 607.5 ms (28.7 GB/s), 239.6 ms with no kernel running.
GPU-to-GPU copies from GPU memory on GPU queue 16: 17.84 GB in 21.5 ms (831.6 GB/s), 21.5 ms with no kernel running.
Host-to-GPU copies from pinned host memory on GPU queue 14: 0.24 GB in 9.7 ms (24.9 GB/s), 9.7 ms with no kernel running.
GPU-to-host copies from GPU memory on GPU queue 14: 0.24 GB in 8.4 ms (28.3 GB/s), 8.4 ms with no kernel running.
Copies on different GPU queues overlap each other, so their times with no kernel running add up to more than the copy total.

A GPU queue (a stream) runs its work in order; copies and kernels on different queues can overlap. Pinned host memory is locked in RAM, so the GPU reads it directly; ordinary (pageable) memory is first staged through a pinned buffer.
